frameworks.name: Zero-to-$100M Stage Roadmap
frameworks.definition: A 10-stage roadmap from zero to $100M+ in revenue, broken down by eight business functions per stage, covering symptoms of each constraint and the steps taken to graduate through it, validated across software, physical products, service businesses, and brick-and-mortar.

claims.text: According to Alex Hormozi, most critics who attempt to deter you from extraordinary effort do so because your failure would validate the risk they themselves chose not to take — their discouragement is self-protective, not concern for your welfare.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: The critic has not taken the same or comparable risk themselves
The person being criticized is pursuing an unconventional or high-effort path
claims.mechanism: A critic who chose not to take a risk experiences cognitive dissonance if others succeed taking that risk; discouraging others preemptively resolves that dissonance by preventing the comparison.
bounded_by: Does not apply to critics who have personal experience with the specific risk domain and raise evidence-based concerns

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that ordinary people will naturally try to keep extraordinary-aspirants at average performance levels, because extraordinary behavior appears excessive or unreasonable when judged by ordinary standards.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: The person pursuing extraordinary results is embedded in a social circle of average performers
claims.mechanism: Ordinary people use their own behavior as the reference benchmark; actions that deviate sharply from that benchmark are interpreted as excessive rather than aspirational, triggering social correction pressure.
bounded_by: Does not apply when the social environment consists of high-performers using similarly ambitious benchmarks

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that advice-seekers should weight input from people who are closest to their goals — who have navigated the specific path — rather than from people who are emotionally closest (friends, family) but lack relevant experience.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: The decision involves a high-stakes, high-uncertainty path
A gap exists between those with goal-proximity and those with emotional proximity
claims.mechanism: People with emotional proximity but no relevant experience apply generic social norms; people with goal-proximity have empirical data about which actions actually produce the target outcome.
bounded_by: Does not apply when emotional-proximity advisors also have relevant goal-proximity experience

examples.text: Alex Hormozi offers a reductio ad mortem reframe for critic-anxiety: critics will eventually die, and their opinion will carry no weight then. Since death eliminates the relevance of their judgment, the judgment was not meaningfully relevant in the first place. This is offered as a way to dissolve the emotional grip of critic opinions rather than as an empirical argument.

practices.text: Ignore critics who lack direct experience with the risk or path you are pursuing; do not let social deterrence from average performers redirect your effort.
When seeking advice, deliberately seek out people who are closest to your specific goal — not those who are emotionally closest — and weight their input proportionally higher.
